In sum, those of us working on tech and AI policy will benefit immensely from Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas. Neither a screed against technology nor a blind endorsement of it, the encyclical properly frames the benefits and challenges of technology, and calls us to a timeless aim: focusing on our families, our local institutions—and our own interior lives—as we also work, through our governments, to maintain human dignity during an era of historic technological transformation.

Pope Leo XIV concludes Magnifica Humanitas with a stirring reminder of the “grandeur of humanity,” a principle that ought to guide any AI policy: “For this reason, as a believer among believers, I invite everyone to contemplate, in the face of the Son of God, the grandeur of humanity that shines a light also on the era of AI. In Christ, we are called to cooperate in the work of creation, rather than be disinterested observers of technological processes that limit our freedom and responsibility.

Magnifica Humanitas also reminds us of the enduring dignity of work, even—especially—in a time of digital transformation: “work is not simply an instrument; it expresses and enhances the dignity of our lives. It is a requirement of the human condition, a normal path toward maturity, development and personal fulfillment.”

Pope Leo XIV, refreshingly, leans heavily on Augustine in his analysis of the limits of the secular order, especially in light of the challenges presented by AI: “Saint Augustine described human history as a struggle between two loves, which give rise to two ways of inhabiting the world and living together — or two ‘cities,’  as it were: on the one hand, the love of God and neighbor; on the other, the exclusive love of self. ‘Two loves have built two cities: the earthly city, the love of self ev

The extended section on the PRINCIPLE OF SUBSIDIARITY is a must-read, as Pope Leo explains the necessity of institutions other than national governments being involved in tech and AI policy-making: “In this context, States and transnational institutions are called to ensure fair rules and effective safeguards, so that local communities, intermediary organizations, schools, universities, religious institutions and associations have a voice and can contribute to the discernment of choices that aff

Invoking two powerful episodes from Scripture—the Tower of Babel and the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem—the Holy Father charts a possible path: “The risk of dehumanization — of building a future that excludes God and reduces the other to a means — is an ancient and ever-new temptation that today takes on a technical guise. Instead, let us choose the ‘way of Nehemiah,’ which highlights the importance of working together to make the City of God a safe place for returning exiles.”

Leo identifies yet another challenge—the sheer pace of technological developments: “We are living through a rapid phase of transition, a ‘change of era,’ in which — while some are vying for the future of new technologies and others dedicate themselves to reflecting on the matter — most people are watching and waiting, observing from afar and merely hoping for the best. For this very reason, crucial questions impose themselves on our conscience and can no longer be avoided: Where are we going? To

Pope Leo also discusses a concern that many of us have regarding the sheer size (and therefore power) of some of the companies developing AI: “the main drivers of development are private, often transnational, parties that are endowed with resources and the capacity to intervene that surpass those of many Governments. Technological power thus takes on an unprecedented, predominantly “private” aspect, which makes it even more challenging to discern, govern and direct such power toward the common g
